{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
{{Short description|Mathematics glossary}}
This is a glossary of properties and concepts in [[algebraic topology]] in mathematics.

See also: [[glossary of topology]], [[list of algebraic topology topics]], [[glossary of category theory]], [[glossary of differential geometry and topology]], [[timeline of manifolds]].

*'''Convention''': Throughout the article, ''I'' denotes the unit interval, ''S''<sup>''n''</sup> the [[n-sphere|''n''-sphere]] and ''D''<sup>''n''</sup> the ''n''-disk. Also, throughout the article, spaces are assumed to be '''reasonable'''; this can be taken to mean for example, a space is a CW complex or [[compactly generated space|compactly generated]] [[weakly Hausdorff space]]. Similarly, no attempt is made to be definitive about the definition of a [[spectrum (topology)|spectrum]]. A [[simplicial set]] is not thought of as a space; i.e., we generally distinguish between simplicial sets and their geometric realizations.
*'''Inclusion criterion''': As there is no [[glossary of homological algebra]] in Wikipedia right now, this glossary also includes a few concepts in homological algebra (e.g., chain homotopy); some concepts in [[geometric topology]] and [[differential topology]] are also fair game. On the other hand, the items that appear in [[glossary of topology]] are generally omitted. [[Abstract homotopy theory]] and [[motivic homotopy theory]] are also outside the scope. [[Glossary of category theory]] covers (or will cover) concepts in theory of [[model category|model categories]]. See the [[glossary of symplectic geometry]] for the topics in symplectic topology such as quantization.

{{compact ToC|side=yes|sym=yes}}

==!$@==

{{glossary}}

{{term|*}}
{{defn|1=The base point of a based space.}}

{{term|<math>X_+</math>}}
{{defn|1=For an unbased space ''X'', ''X''<sub>+</sub> is the based space obtained by adjoining a disjoint base point.}}

{{glossary end}}

== A ==

{{glossary}}
{{term|absolute neighborhood retract}}
{{defn|1=An [[absolute neighborhood retract]] is used as an alternative to a CW-complex as a nice space (the homotopy type of an ANR and that of a CW-complex are the same).}}

{{term|abstract}}
{{defn|no=1|Abstract homotopy theory}}

{{term|Adams}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[John Frank Adams]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[Adams spectral sequence]].}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The [[Adams conjecture]].}}
{{defn|no=4|1=The [[Adams e-invariant|Adams ''e''-invariant]].}}
{{defn|no=5|1=The [[Adams operations]].}}

{{term|Alexander duality}}
{{defn|1=[[Alexander duality]]}}

{{term|Alexander trick}}
{{defn|The [[Alexander trick]]  produces a section of the restriction map <math>\operatorname{Top}(D^{n+1}) \to \operatorname{Top}(S^n)</math>, Top denoting a [[homeomorphism group]]; namely, the section is given by sending a homeomorphism <math>f: S^n \to S^n</math> to the homeomorphism
:<math>\widetilde{f}: D^{n+1} \to D^{n+1}, \, 0 \mapsto 0, 0 \ne x \mapsto |x|f(x/|x|)</math>.
This section is in fact a homotopy inverse.<ref>Let ''r'', ''s'' denote the restriction and the section. For each ''f'' in <math>\operatorname{Top}(D^{n+1})</math>, define <math>h_t(f)(x) = tf(x/t), |x| \le t, h_t(f)(x) = |x|f(x/|x|), |x| > t</math>. Then <math>h_t: s \circ r \sim \operatorname{id}</math>.</ref>}}

{{term|Analysis Situs}}
{{defn|1=''[[Analysis Situs]]''.}}

{{term|annulus}}
{{defn|1=The [[annulus theorem]].}}

{{term|[[approximate fibration]]}}
{{defn|no=1|1=An [[approximate fibration]], a generalization of a fibration and a projection in a locally trivial bundle.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A [[manifold approximate fibration]] is a proper approximate fibration between manifolds.}}

{{term|aspherical space}}
{{defn|1=[[Aspherical space]]}}

{{term|assembly map}}

{{term|Atiyah}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Michael Atiyah]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Atiyah duality]].}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The [[Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== B ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|bar construction}}

{{term|based space}}
{{defn|1=A pair (''X'', ''x''<sub>0</sub>) consisting of a space ''X'' and a point ''x''<sub>0</sub> in ''X''.}}

{{term|Betti number}}
{{defn|1=See [[Betti number]].}}
{{term|Bing–Borsuk conjecture}}
{{defn|1=See [[Bing–Borsuk conjecture]].}}

{{term|Bockstein homomorphism}}

{{term|Borel}}
{{defn|1=[[Borel conjecture]].}}

{{term|Borel–Moore homology}}

{{term|Borsuk's theorem}}

{{term|Bott}}
{{defn|no=1|[[Raoul Bott]].}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[Bott periodicity theorem]] for unitary groups say: <math>\pi_q U = \pi_{q+2} U, q \ge 0</math>.}}
{{defn|no=3|The [[Bott periodicity theorem]] for orthogonal groups say: <math>\pi_q O = \pi_{q+8} O, q \ge 0</math>.}}

{{term|Brouwer fixed-point theorem}}
{{defn|1=The [[Brouwer fixed-point theorem]] says that any map <math>f: D^n \to D^n</math> has a fixed point.}}

{{term|Brown–Peterson spectrum}}
{{defn|1=The [[Brown–Peterson spectrum]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== C ==

{{glossary}}
{{term|cap product}}

{{term|Casson}}
{{defn|[[Casson invariant]].}}

{{term|Čech cohomology}}

{{term|cellular}}
{{defn|no=1|A map ƒ:''X''→''Y'' between CW complexes is [[cellular map|cellular]] if <math>f(X^n) \subset Y^n</math> for all ''n''.}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[cellular approximation theorem]] says that every map between CW complexes is homotopic to a [[cellular map]] between them.}}
{{defn|no=3|The  [[cellular homology]] is the (canonical) homology of a CW complex. Note it applies to CW complexes and not to spaces in general. A cellular homology is highly computable; it is especially useful for spaces with natural cell decompositions like projective spaces or Grassmannian.}}

{{term|chain homotopy}}
{{defn|1=Given chain maps <math>f, g: (C, d_C) \to (D, d_D)</math> between chain complexes of modules, a [[chain homotopy]] ''s'' from ''f'' to ''g'' is a sequence of module homomorphisms <math>s_i: C_i \to D_{i+1}</math> satisfying <math>f_i - g_i = d_D \circ s_i + s_{i-1} \circ d_C</math>. It is also called a [[homotopy operator]].}}

{{term|chain map}}
{{defn|1=A chain map <math>f: (C, d_C) \to (D, d_D)</math> between chain complexes of modules is a sequence of module homomorphisms <math>f_i: C_i \to D_i</math> that commutes with the differentials; i.e., <math>d_D \circ f_i = f_{i-1} \circ d_C</math>.}}

{{term|chain homotopy equivalence}}
{{defn|1=A chain map that is an isomorphism up to chain homotopy; that is, if ''ƒ'':''C''→''D'' is a chain map, then it is a chain homotopy equivalence if there is a chain map ''g'':''D''→''C'' such that ''g''ƒ and ƒ''g'' are chain homotopic to the identity homomorphisms on ''C'' and ''D'', respectively.}}

{{term|change of fiber}}
{{defn|The [[change of fiber]] of a fibration ''p'' is a homotopy equivalence, up to homotopy, between the fibers of ''p'' induced by a path in the base.}}

{{term|character variety}}
{{defn|1=The [[character variety]]<ref>Despite the name, it may not be an [[algebraic variety]] in the strict sense; for example, it may not be irreducible. Also, without some finiteness assumption on ''G'', it is only a scheme.</ref> of a group π and an algebraic group ''G'' (e.g., a reductive complex Lie group) is the [[geometric invariant theory quotient]] by ''G'':
:<math>\mathcal{X}(\pi, G) = \operatorname{Hom}(\pi, G)/ \! /G</math>.}}

{{term|characteristic class}}
{{defn|1=Let Vect(''X'') be the set of isomorphism classes of vector bundles on ''X''. We can view <math>X \mapsto \operatorname{Vect}(X)</math> as a contravariant functor from '''Top''' to '''Set''' by sending a map ƒ:''X'' → ''Y'' to the pullback ƒ<sup>*</sup> along it. Then a [[characteristic class]] is a [[natural transformation]] from Vect to the cohomology functor H<sup>*</sup>. Explicitly, to each vector bundle ''E'' we assign a cohomology class, say, ''c''(''E''). The assignment is natural in the sense that ƒ<sup>*</sup>c(''E'') = c(ƒ<sup>*</sup>''E'').}}

{{term|chromatic homotopy theory}}
{{defn|1=[[chromatic homotopy theory]].}}

{{term|class}}
{{defn|no=1|[[Chern class]].}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Stiefel–Whitney class]].}}

{{term|classifying space}}
{{defn|1=Loosely speaking, a [[classifying space]] is a space representing some contravariant functor defined on the category of spaces; for example, <math>BU</math> is the classifying space in the sense <math>[-, BU]</math> is the functor <math>X \mapsto \operatorname{Vect}^{\mathbb{R}}(X)</math> that sends a space to the set of isomorphism classes of real vector bundles on the space.}}

{{term|clutching}}

{{term|cobar spectral sequence}}

{{term|cobordism}}
{{defn|no=1|1=See [[cobordism]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A [[cobordism ring]] is a ring whose elements are cobordism classes.}}
{{defn|no=3|See also [[h-cobordism theorem]], [[s-cobordism theorem]].}}

{{term|coefficient ring}}
{{defn|1=If ''E'' is a ring spectrum, then the coefficient ring of it is the ring <math>\pi_* E</math>.}}

{{term|cofiber sequence}}
{{defn|1=A cofiber sequence is any sequence that is equivalent to the sequence <math >X \overset{f}\to Y \to C_f</math> for some ƒ where <math>C_f</math> is the reduced mapping cone of ƒ (called the cofiber of ƒ).}}

{{term|cofibrant approximation}}

{{term|cofibration}}
{{defn|1=A map <math>i: A \to B</math> is a [[cofibration]] if it satisfies the property: given <math>h_0: B \to X</math> and homotopy <math>g_t: A \to X</math> such that <math>g_0=h_0\circ i</math>, there is a homotopy <math>h_t: B \to X</math> such that <math>h_t \circ i = g_t</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Hatcher|loc=Ch. 4. H.}}</ref> A cofibration is injective and is a homeomorphism onto its image.}}

{{term|coherent homotopy}}

{{term|coherency}}
{{defn|1=See [[coherency (homotopy theory)]]}}

{{term|cohomotopy group}}
{{defn|1=For a based space ''X'', the set of homotopy classes <math>[X, S^n]</math> is called the ''n''-th [[cohomotopy group]] of ''X''.}}

{{term|cohomology operation}}

{{term|collapse}}
{{defn|1=An informal phrase but usually means taking a quotient; e.g., a cone is obtained by collapsing the top (or bottom) of a cylinder.}}

{{term|collar}}
{{defn|1=[[collar neighbourhood]]}}

{{term|completion}}

{{term|complex bordism}}

{{term|complex-oriented}}
{{defn|1=A multiplicative cohomology theory ''E'' is [[complex-oriented cohomology theory|complex-oriented]] if the restriction map ''E''<sup>2</sup>('''C'''''P''<sup>∞</sup>) → ''E''<sup>2</sup>('''C'''''P''<sup>1</sup>) is surjective.}}

{{term|concordant}}

{{term|cone}}
{{defn|1=The [[cone (topology)|cone]] over a space ''X'' is <math>CX = X \times I / X \times \{0\}</math>. The [[reduced cone]] is obtained from the [[reduced cylinder]] <math>X \wedge I_+</math> by collapsing the top.}}

{{term|connective}}
{{defn|A spectrum ''E'' is [[connective spectrum|connective]] if <math>\pi_q E = 0</math> for all negative integers ''q''.}}

{{term|configuration space}}

{{term|1=constant}}
{{defn|1=A [[constant sheaf]] on a space ''X'' is a sheaf <math>\mathcal{F}</math> on ''X'' such that for some set ''A'' and some map <math>A \to \mathcal{F}(X)</math>, the natural map <math>A \to \mathcal{F}(X) \to \mathcal{F}_x</math> is bijective for any ''x'' in ''X''.}}

{{term|1=continuous}}
{{defn|1=[[Continuous cohomology]].}}

{{term|contractible space}}
{{defn|1=A space is [[contractible space|contractible]] if the identity map on the space is homotopic to the constant map.}}

{{term|covering}}
{{defn|no=1|A map ''p'': ''Y'' → ''X'' is a [[covering space|covering]] or a covering map if each point of ''x'' has a neighborhood ''N'' that is [[evenly covered]] by ''p''; this means that the pre-image of ''N'' is a disjoint union of open sets, each of which maps to ''N'' homeomorphically.}}
{{defn|no=2|It is ''n''-sheeted if each fiber ''p''<sup>−1</sup>(''x'') has exactly ''n'' elements.}}
{{defn|no=3|It is [[universal covering|universal]] if ''Y'' is simply connected.}}
{{defn|no=4|A morphism of a covering is a map over ''X''. In particular, an automorphism of a covering ''p'':''Y''→''X'' (also called a [[deck transformation]]) is a map ''Y''→''Y'' over ''X'' that has inverse; i.e., a homeomorphism over ''X''.}}
{{defn|no=5|A [[G-covering|''G''-covering]] is a covering arising from a [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] on a space ''X'' by a group ''G'', the covering map being the quotient map from ''X'' to the [[orbit space]] ''X/G''. The notion is used to state the universal property: if ''X'' admits a universal covering (in particular connected), then
::<math>\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(X, x_0), G)</math> is the set of isomorphism classes of ''G''-coverings.
:In particular, if ''G'' is abelian, then the left-hand side is <math>\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(X, x_0), G) = \operatorname{H}^1(X; G)</math> (cf. [[nonabelian cohomology]].)}}
{{defn|no=6|[[covering dimension]].}}

{{term|cup product}}

{{term|CW complex}}
{{defn|1=A [[CW complex]] is a space ''X'' equipped with a CW structure; i.e., a filtration
::<math>X^0 \subset X^1 \subset X^2 \subset \cdots \subset X</math>
:such that (1) ''X''<sup>0</sup> is discrete and (2) ''X''<sup>''n''</sup> is obtained from ''X''<sup>''n''-1</sup> by attaching ''n''-cells.}}

{{term|cyclic homology}}

{{glossary end}}

== D ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|deck transformation}}
{{defn|Another term for an automorphism of a covering.}}

{{term|deformation retract}}
{{defn|A subspace <math>A \subset X</math> is called a [[deformation retract]] of ''X'' if there is a homotopy <math>h_t : X \to X</math> such that <math>h_0</math> is the identity, <math>h_1(X) \subset A</math> and <math>{h_1}|_A</math> is the identity (i.e., <math>h_1</math> is a [[retract (category theory)|retract]] of <math>A \hookrightarrow X</math> in the sense in category theory). It is called a [[strong deformation retract]] if, in addition, <math>h_t</math> satisfies the requirement that <math>{h_t}|_A</math> is the identity. For example, a homotopy <math>h_t : B \to B, \, x \mapsto (1-t)x</math> exhibits that the origin is a strong deformation retract of an open ball ''B'' centered at the origin.}}

{{term|Deligne–Beilinson cohomology}}
{{defn|1=[[Deligne–Beilinson cohomology]]}}

{{term|delooping}}

{{term|degeneracy cycle}}

{{term|degree}}

{{term|de Rham}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[de Rham cohomology]], the cohomology of complex of differential forms.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[de Rham theorem]] gives an explicit isomorphism between the de Rham cohomology and the singular cohomology.}}

{{term|disjoint disk property}}
{{defn|1=[[disjoint disk property]].}}

{{term|Dold}}
{{defn|1=The [[Dold–Thom theorem]].}}

{{term|dominate}}
{{defn|1=A space <math>Y</math> is said to [[dominate (topology)|dominate]] a space <math>X</math> if there are <math>p : Y \to X</math> and <math>g : X \to Y</math> such that <math>p \circ g : X \to X</math> is homotopic to the identity.}}

{{glossary end}}

== E ==
{{glossary}}
{{term|Eckmann–Hilton argument}}
{{defn|1=The [[Eckmann–Hilton argument]].}}

{{term|Eckmann–Hilton duality}}

{{term|Eilenberg–MacLane spaces}}
{{defn|1=Given an abelian group π, the [[Eilenberg–MacLane spaces]] <math>K(\pi, n)</math> are characterized by
:<math>\pi_q K(\pi, n)=
\begin{cases}
\pi & \text{if } q = n \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}</math>.}}

{{term|Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms}}
{{defn|1=The [[Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms]] are the set of axioms that any cohomology theory (singular, cellular, etc.) must satisfy. Weakening the axioms (namely dropping the dimension axiom) leads to a [[generalized cohomology theory]].}}

{{term|Eilenberg–Zilber theorem}}

{{term|elliptic}}
{{defn|[[elliptic cohomology]].}}

{{term|1=E_n-algebra|2=E<sub>''n''</sub>-algebra}}

{{term|equivariant algebraic topology}}
{{defn|1=[[Equivariant algebraic topoloy]] is the study of spaces with [[continuous group action|(continuous) group action]].}}

{{term|etale}}
{{defn|1=[[étale homotopy]].}}

{{term|Euclidean}}
{{defn|A [[Euclidean neighborhood retract]]}}

{{term|exact}}
{{defn|1=A sequence of pointed sets <math>X \overset{f}\to Y \overset{g}\to Z</math> is [[exact sequence|exact]] if the image of ''f'' coincides with the pre-image of the chosen point of ''Z''.}}

{{term|excision}}
{{defn|1=The [[excision theorem|excision]] axiom for homology says: if <math>U \subset X</math> and <math>\overline{U} \subset \operatorname{int}(A)</math>, then for each ''q'',
::<math>\operatorname{H}_q(X-U,A-U) \to \operatorname{H}_q(X,A)</math>
:is an isomorphism.}}

{{term|excisive pair/triad}}

{{glossary end}}

== F ==

{{glossary}}
{{term|factorization homology}}

{{term|fiber-homotopy equivalence}}
{{defn|1=Given ''D''→''B'', ''E''→''B'', a map ƒ:''D''→''E'' over ''B'' is a [[fiber-homotopy equivalence]] if it is invertible up to homotopy over ''B''. The basic fact is that if ''D''→''B'', ''E''→''B'' are fibrations, then a homotopy equivalence from ''D'' to ''E'' is a fiber-homotopy equivalence.}}

{{term|fiber sequence}}
{{defn|1=The [[fiber sequence]] of a map <math>f: X \to Y</math> is the sequence <math>F_f \overset{p} \to X \overset{f}\to Y</math> where <math>F_f \overset{p} \to X</math> is the homotopy fiber of ''f''; i.e., the pullback of the path space fibration <math>PY \to Y</math> along ''f''.}}

{{term|fiber square}}
{{defn|1=[[fiber square]]}}

{{term|fibration}}
{{defn|1=A map ''p'':''E'' → ''B'' is a [[fibration]] if for any given homotopy <math>g_t: X \to B</math> and a map <math>h_0: X \to E</math> such that <math>p \circ h_0 = g_0</math>, there exists a homotopy <math>h_t: X \to E</math> such that <math>p \circ h_t = g_t</math>. (The above property is called the [[homotopy lifting property]].) A covering map is a basic example of a fibration.}}

{{term|fibration sequence}}
{{defn|1=One says <math>F \to X \overset{p}\to B</math> is a fibration sequence to mean that ''p'' is a fibration and that ''F'' is homotopy equivalent to the homotopy fiber of ''p'', with some understanding of base points.}}

{{term|finitely dominated}}

{{term|fundamental class}}

{{term|fundamental group}}
{{defn|1=The [[fundamental group]] of a space ''X'' with base point ''x''<sub>0</sub> is the group of homotopy classes of loops at ''x''<sub>0</sub>. It is precisely the first homotopy group of (''X'', ''x''<sub>0</sub>) and is thus denoted by <math>\pi_1(X, x_0)</math>.}}

{{term|fundamental groupoid}}
{{defn|1=The [[fundamental groupoid]] of a space ''X'' is the category whose objects are the points of ''X'' and whose morphisms ''x'' → ''y'' are the homotopy classes of paths from ''x'' to ''y''; thus, the set of all morphisms from an object ''x''<sub>0</sub> to itself is, by definition, the fundamental group <math>\pi_1(X, x_0)</math>.}}

{{term|framed}}
{{defn|1=A [[framed manifold]] is a manifold with a framing.}}

{{term|free}}
{{defn|1=Synonymous with unbased. For example, the [[free path space]] of a space ''X'' refers to the space of all maps from ''I'' to ''X''; i.e., <math>X^I</math> while the path space of a based space ''X'' consists of such map that preserve the base point (i.e., 0 goes to the base point of ''X'').}}

{{term|Freedman}}
{{defn|1=Freedman's [[E8 manifold]].}}

{{term|Freudenthal suspension theorem}}
{{defn|1=For a nondegenerately based space ''X'', the [[Freudenthal suspension theorem]] says: if ''X'' is (''n''-1)-connected, then the suspension homomorphism
:<math>\pi_q X \to \pi_{q+1} \Sigma X</math>
is bijective for ''q'' < 2''n'' - 1 and is surjective if ''q'' = 2''n'' - 1.}}

{{term|Fulton–MacPherson compactification}}
{{defn|The [[Fulton–MacPherson compactification]] of the [[configuration space (mathematics)|configuration space]] of ''n'' distinct labeled points in a compact complex manifold is a natural smooth compactification introduced by Fulton and MacPherson.}}

{{glossary end}}

== G ==
{{glossary}}
{{term|G-fibration}}
{{defn|1=A [[G-fibration]] with some [[topological monoid]] ''G''. An example is [[Moore's path space fibration]].}}

{{term|G-space}}
{{defn|1=A [[G-space]] is a space together with an action of a group ''G'' (usually satisfying some conditions).}}

{{term|Γ-space}}

{{term|generalized cohomology theory}}
{{defn|1=A [[generalized cohomology theory]] is a contravariant functor from the category of pairs of spaces to the category of abelian groups that satisfies all of the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms except the dimension axiom.}}

{{term|geometrization conjecture}}
{{defn|1=[[geometrization conjecture]]}}

{{term|genus}}

{{term|germ}}
{{defn|1=[[germ (mathematics)|germ]]}}

{{term|group completion}} 
{{term|grouplike}}
{{defn|1=An H-space ''X'' is said to be '''group-like''' or '''grouplike''' if <math>\pi_0 X</math> is a [[group (mathematics)|group]]; i.e., ''X'' satisfies the group axioms up to homotopy.}}

{{term|Gysin sequence}}

{{glossary end}}

== H ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Hauptvermutung}}
{{defn|no=1|''[[Hauptvermutung]]'', a German for main conjecture, is short for ''die Hauptvermutung der kombinatorischen Topologie'' (the main conjecture of combinatorial topology). It asks whether two simplicial complexes are isomorphic if homeomorphic. It was disproved by Milnor in 1961.}}
{{defn|no=2|There are some variants; for example, one can ask whether two PL manifolds are PL-isomorphic if homeomorphic (which is also false).}}

{{term|h-cobordism}}
{{defn|1=[[h-cobordism]].}}

{{term|Hilton–Milnor theorem}}
{{defn|1=The [[Hilton–Milnor theorem]].}}

{{term|Hirzebruch}}
{{defn|[[Hirzebruch signature theorem]].}}

{{term|H-space}}
{{defn|1=An [[H-space]] is a based space that is a [[unital magma]] up to homotopy.}}

{{term|Hodge}}
{{defn|1=The [[Hodge spectral sequence]].}}

{{term|homologous}}
{{defn|1=Two cycles are homologous if they belong to the same homology class.}}

{{term|homology manifold}}
{{defn|1=A [[homology manifold]] is a space that looks like a topological manifold, homology-theory speaking.}}

{{term|homology sphere}}
{{defn|A [[homology sphere]] is a manifold having the homology type of a sphere.}}

{{term|homotopy category}}
{{defn|1=Let ''C'' be a subcategory of the category of all spaces. Then the [[homotopy category]] of ''C'' is the category whose class of objects is the same as the class of objects of ''C'' but the set of morphisms from an object ''x'' to an object ''y'' is the set of the homotopy classes of morphisms from ''x'' to ''y'' in ''C''. For example, a map is a homotopy equivalence if and only if it is an isomorphism in the homotopy category.}}

{{term|homotopy colimit}}
{{defn|A [[homotopy colimit]] is a homotopically-correct version of colimit.}}

{{term|homotopy over a space ''B''}}
{{defn|A homotopy ''h''<sub>''t''</sub> such that for each fixed ''t'', ''h''<sub>''t''</sub> is a map over ''B''.}}

{{term|homotopy equivalence}}
{{defn|no=1|A map ƒ:''X''→''Y'' is a [[homotopy equivalence]] if it is invertible up to homotopy; that is, there exists a map g: ''Y''→''X'' such that ''g'' ∘ ƒ is homotopic to th identity map on ''X'' and ƒ ∘ ''g'' is homotopic to the identity map on ''Y''.}}
{{defn|no=2|Two spaces are said to be homotopy equivalent if there is a homotopy equivalence between the two. For example, by definition, a space is contractible if it is homotopy equivalent to a [[point space]].}}

{{term|homotopy excision theorem}}
{{defn|1=The [[homotopy excision theorem]] is a substitute for the failure of excision for homotopy groups.}}

{{term|homotopy fiber}}
{{defn|1=The [[homotopy fiber]] of a based map ƒ:''X''→''Y'', denoted by ''F''ƒ, is the pullback of <math>PY \to Y, \, \chi \mapsto \chi(1)</math> along ''f''.}}

{{term|homotopy fiber product}}
{{defn|1=A fiber product is a particular kind of a [[limit (category theory)|limit]]. Replacing this limit lim with a [[homotopy limit]] holim yields a [[homotopy fiber product]].}}

{{term|homotopy group}}
{{defn|no=1|For a based space ''X'', let <math>\pi_n X = [S^n, X]</math>, the set of homotopy classes of based maps. Then <math>\pi_0 X</math> is the set of path-connected components of ''X'', <math>\pi_1 X</math> is the fundamental group of ''X'' and <math>\pi_n X, \, n \ge 2</math> are the (higher) ''n''-th [[homotopy group]]s of ''X''.}}
{{defn|no=2|For based spaces <math>A \subset X</math>, the [[relative homotopy group]] <math>\pi_n(X, A)</math> is defined as <math>\pi_{n-1}</math> of the space of paths that all start at the base point of ''X'' and end somewhere in ''A''. Equivalently, it is the <math>\pi_{n-1}</math> of the homotopy fiber of <math>A \hookrightarrow X</math>.}}
{{defn|no=3|If ''E'' is a spectrum, then <math>\pi_k E = \varinjlim_{n} \pi_{k + n} E_n.</math>}}
{{defn|no=4|If ''X'' is a based space, then the [[stable homotopy group|stable ''k''-th homotopy group]] of ''X'' is <math>\pi_k^s X = \varinjlim_{n} \pi_{k + n} \Sigma^n X</math>. In other words, it is the ''k''-th homotopy group of the suspension spectrum of ''X''.}}

{{term|homotopy pullback}}
{{defn|1=A [[homotopy pullback]] is a special case of a homotopy limit that is a homotopically-correct pullback.}}

{{term|homotopy quotient}}
{{defn|1=If ''G'' is a [[Lie group]] acting on a manifold ''X'', then the quotient space <math>(EG \times X)/G</math> is called the [[homotopy quotient]] (or Borel construction) of ''X'' by ''G'', where ''EG'' is the universal bundle of ''G''.}}

{{term|homotopy spectral sequence}}

{{term|homotopy sphere}}
{{defn|A [[homotopy sphere]] is a manifold having the homotopy type of a sphere.}}

{{term|Hopf}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Heinz Hopf]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Hopf invariant]].}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The [[Hopf index theorem]].}}
{{defn|no=4|1=[[Hopf construction]].}}

{{term|Hurewicz}}
{{defn|1=The [[Hurewicz theorem]] establishes a relationship between homotopy groups and homology groups.}}

{{glossary end}}

== I ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|infinite loop space}}

{{term|infinite loop space machine}}
{{defn|1=[[Infinite loop space machine]].}}

{{term|infinite mapping telescope}}

{{term|intersection}}
{{defn|1=[[intersection pairing]].}}
{{defn|1=[[intersection homology]], a substitute for an ordinary (singular) homology for a singular space.}}
{{defn|1=[[intersection cohomology]]}}

{{term|integration along the fiber}}
{{defn|See [[integration along the fiber]].}}

{{term|invariance of domain}}
{{defn|[[invariance of domain]].}}

{{term|isotopy}}

{{glossary end}}

== J ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|J-homomorphism}}
{{defn|See [[J-homomorphism]].}}

{{term|join}}
{{defn|The [[join (topology)|join]] of based spaces ''X'', ''Y'' is <math>X \star Y = \Sigma(X\wedge Y).</math>}}

{{glossary end}}

== K ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|''k''-invariant}}

{{term|Kan complex}}
{{defn|See [[Kan complex]].}}

{{term|Kirby–Siebenmann}}
{{defn|[[Kirby–Siebenmann classification]].}}

{{term|Kervaire invariant}}
{{defn|1=The [[Kervaire invariant]].}}

{{term|Koszul duality}}
{{defn|1=[[Koszul duality]].}}

{{term|Kuiper}}
{{defn|[[Kuiper's theorem]] says that the general linear group of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is contractible.}}

{{term|Künneth formula}}

{{glossary end}}

== L ==

{{glossary}}
{{term|L-class}}
{{defn|1=[[L-class (mathematics)|L-class]].}}

{{term|Lazard ring}}
{{defn|1=The [[Lazard ring]] ''L'' is the (huge) commutative ring together with the [[formal group law]] ƒ that is universal among all the formal group laws in the sense that any formal group law ''g'' over a commutative ring ''R'' is obtained via a ring homomorphism ''L'' → ''R'' mapping ƒ to ''g''. According to Quillen's theorem, it is also the coefficient ring of the [[complex bordism]] MU. The [[spectrum of a ring|Spec]] of ''L'' is called the [[moduli space of formal group laws]].}}

{{term|Lefschetz}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Solomon Lefschetz]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[Lefschetz fixed-point theorem]] says: given a finite simplicial complex ''K'' and its geometric realization ''X'', if a map <math>f: X \to X</math> has no fixed point, then the Lefschetz number of ''f''; that is,
:<math>\sum_0^\infty (-1)^q \operatorname{tr}(f_*: \operatorname{H}_q(X) \to \operatorname{H}_q(X))</math>
is zero. For example, it implies the [[Brouwer fixed-point theorem]] since the Lefschetz number of <math>f: D^n \to D^n</math> is, as higher homologies vanish, one.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The [[Lefschetz hyperplane theorem]].}}

{{term|lens space}}
{{defn|1=The [[lens space]] is the quotient space <math>\{ z \in \mathbb{C}^n | |z| = 1 \}/ \mu_p</math> where <math>\mu_p</math> is the group of ''p''-th roots of unity acting on the unit sphere by <math>\zeta \cdot (z_1, \dots, z_n) = (\zeta z_1, \dots, \zeta z_n)</math>.}}

{{term|Leray spectral sequence}}

{{term|content=''L''<sup>2</sup>}}
{{defn|1=The [[L2-cohomology|''L''<sup>2</sup>-cohomology]] of a [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian]] or [[Kähler manifold]] is the cohomology of the complexes of differential forms with [[square-integrable]] coefficients (coefficients for forms not cohomology).}}

{{term|local coefficient}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A module over the [[group ring]] <math>\mathbb{Z}[\pi_1 B]</math> for some based space ''B''; in other words, an abelian group together with a homomorphism <math>\pi_1 B \to \operatorname{Aut}(A)</math>.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[local coefficient system]] over a based space ''B'' with an abelian group ''A'' is a fiber bundle over ''B'' with discrete fiber ''A''. If ''B'' admits a universal covering <math>\widetilde{B}</math>, then this meaning coincides with that of 1. in the sense: every local coefficient system over ''B'' can be given as the [[associated bundle]] <math>\widetilde{B} \times_{\pi_1 B} A</math>.}}

{{term|local invariant}}
{{defn|[[Local invariant cycle theorem]].}}

{{term|local sphere}}
{{defn|1=The localization of a sphere at some prime number}}

{{term|local system}}
{{defn|1=[[local system]].}}

{{term|localization}}

{{term|locally constant sheaf}}
{{defn|1=A [[locally constant sheaf]] on a space ''X'' is a sheaf such that each point of ''X'' has an open neighborhood on which the sheaf is [[constant sheaf|constant]].}}

{{term|loop space}}
{{defn|The [[loop space]] <math>\Omega X</math> of a based space ''X'' is the space of all loops starting and ending at the base point of ''X''.}}

{{glossary end}}

== M ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Madsen–Weiss theorem}}

{{term|mapping}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[File:Mapping cone.svg|thumb|The mapping cone of a map ƒ:''X''→''Y'' is obtained by gluing the cone over ''X'' to ''Y''.]]The [[mapping cone (topology)|mapping cone]] (or cofiber) of a map ƒ:''X''→''Y'' is <math>C_f = Y \cup_f CX</math>.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[mapping cylinder]] of a map ƒ:''X''→''Y'' is <math>M_f = Y \cup_f (X \times I)</math>. Note: <math>C_f = M_f/(X \times \{0\})</math>.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The reduced versions of the above are obtained by using reduced cone and reduced cylinder.}}
{{defn|no=4|1=The [[mapping path space]] ''P''<sub>''p''</sub> of a map ''p'':''E''→''B'' is the pullback of <math>B^I \to B</math> along ''p''. If ''p'' is fibration, then the natural map ''E''→''P''<sub>''p''</sub> is a [[fiber-homotopy equivalence]]; thus, one can replace ''E'' by the mapping path space without changing the homotopy type of the fiber. A mapping path space is also called a '''mapping cocylinder'''.}}
{{defn|no=5|As a set, the [[mapping space]] from a space ''X'' to a space ''Y'' is the set of all continuous maps from ''X'' to ''Y''. It is topologized in such a way the mapping space is a space; tha is, an object in the category of spaces used in algebraic topology; e.g., the [[category of compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces]]. This topology may or may not be compact-open topology.}}

{{term|Mayer–Vietoris sequence}}

{{term|microbundle}}
{{defn|[[microbundle]]}}

{{term|model category}}
{{defn|1=A presentation of an [[∞-category]].<ref>[https://mathoverflow.net/q/2185 How to think about model categories?]</ref> See also [[model category]].}}

{{term|Moore}}
{{defn|no=1|1=Moore space}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Moore path space]].}}

{{term|multiplicative}}
{{defn|1=A [[generalized cohomology theory]] ''E'' is multiplicative if ''E''<sup>*</sup>(''X'') is a [[graded ring]]. For example, the ordinary cohomology theory and the complex ''K''-theory are multiplicative (in fact, cohomology theories defined by [[E-infinity ring|'''E'''<sub>∞</sub>-rings]] are multiplicative.) }}

{{glossary end}}

== N ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|''n''-cell}}
{{defn|1=Another term for an ''n''-disk.}}

{{term|''n''-connected}}
{{defn|1=A based space ''X'' is [[n-connected|''n''-connected]] if <math>\pi_q X = 0</math> for all integers ''q'' ≤ ''n''. For example, "1-connected" is the same thing as "[[simply connected]]".}}

{{term|''n''-equivalent}}

{{term|NDR-pair}}
{{defn|1=A pair of spaces <math>A \subset X</math> is said to be an [[NDR-pair]] (=neighborhood deformation retract pair) if there is a map <math>u: X \to I</math> and a homotopy <math>h_t: X \to X</math> such that <math>A =u^{-1}(0)</math>, <math>h_0 = \operatorname{id}_X</math>, <math>h_t|_A = \operatorname{id}_A</math> and <math>h_1(\{x | u(x) < 1\}) \subset A</math>.
<br>
If ''A'' is a closed subspace of ''X'', then the pair <math>A \subset X</math> is an NDR-pair if and only if <math>A \hookrightarrow X</math> is a [[cofibration]].</p>}}

{{term|nilpotent}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[nilpotent space]]; for example, a simply connected space is nilpotent.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[nilpotent theorem]].}}

{{term|nonabelian}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[nonabelian cohomology]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[nonabelian algebraic topology]]}}

{{term|normalized}}
{{defn|1=Given a [[simplicial group]] ''G'', the '''normalized chain complex''' ''NG'' of ''G'' is given by <math>(NG)_n = \cap_1^{\infty} \operatorname{ker}d_i^n</math> with the ''n''-th differential given by <math>d^n_0</math>; intuitively, one throws out degenerate chains.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Moore+complex|title = Moore complex in nLab}}</ref> It is also called the '''Moore complex'''.}}

{{glossary end}}

== O ==

{{glossary}}
{{term|obstruction cocycle}}

{{term|obstruction theory}}
{{defn|1=[[Obstruction theory]] is the collection of constructions and calculations indicating when some map on a submanifold (subcomplex) can or cannot be extended to the full manifold. These typically involve the [[Postnikov tower]], [[killing homotopy group]]s, [[obstruction cocycle]]s, etc.}}

{{term|of finite type}}
{{defn|1=A CW complex is of finite type if there are only finitely many cells in each dimension.}}

{{term|operad}}
{{defn|1=The portmanteau of “operations” and “monad”. See [[operad]].}}

{{term|orbibundle}}
{{defn|1=[[orbibundle]].}}

{{term|orbit category}}

{{term|orientation}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[orientation covering]] (or orientation double cover) of a manifold is a two-sheeted covering so that each fiber over ''x'' corresponds to two different ways of orienting a neighborhood of ''x''.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=An [[orientation of a manifold]] is a section of an orientation covering; i.e., a consistent choice of a point in each fiber.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=An [[orientation character]] (also called the first [[Stiefel–Whitney class]]) is a group homomorphism <math>\pi_1(X, x_0) \to \{\pm 1\}</math> that corresponds to an orientation covering of a manifold ''X'' (cf. [[#covering]].)}}
{{defn|no=4|1=See also [[orientation of a vector bundle]] as well as [[orientation sheaf]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== P ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|pair}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[pair (algebraic topology)|pair]] <math>(X, A)</math> of spaces is a space ''X'' together with a subspace <math>A \subset X</math>.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A map of pairs <math>(X, A) \to (Y, B)</math> is a map <math>X \to Y</math> such that <math>f(A) \subset B</math>.}}

{{term|''p''-adic homotopy theory}}
{{defn|1=The [[p-adic homotopy theory|''p''-adic homotopy theory]].}}

{{term|parallelizable}}

{{term|path class}}
{{defn|An equivalence class of paths (two paths are equivalent if they are homotopic to each other).}}

{{term|path lifting}}
{{defn|1=A [[path lifting function]] for a map ''p'': ''E'' → ''B'' is a section of <math>E^I \to P_p</math> where <math>P_p</math> is the [[mapping path space]] of ''p''. For example, a covering is a fibration with a unique path lifting function. By formal consideration, a map is a fibration if and only if there is a path lifting function for it.}}

{{term|path space}}
{{defn|1=The [[path space (algebraic topology)|path space]] of a based space ''X'' is <math>PX = \operatorname{Map}(I, X)</math>, the space of based maps, where the base point of ''I'' is 0. Put in another way, it is the (set-theoretic) fiber of <math>X^I \to X, \, \chi \mapsto \chi(0)</math> over the base point of ''X''. The projection <math>PX \to X, \, \chi \mapsto \chi(1)</math> is called the [[path space fibration]], whose fiber over the base point of ''X'' is the loop space <math>\Omega X</math>. See also [[mapping path space]].}}

{{term|perverse}}
{{defn|1=A [[perverse sheaf]].}}

{{term|phantom map}}
{{defn|[[phantom map]]}}

{{term|piecewise algebraic space}}
{{defn|[[piecewise algebraic space]], the notion introduced by Kontsevich and Soibelman.}}

{{term|PL}}
{{defn|no=1|1=PL short for piecewise linear.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A [[PL manifold]] is a topological manifold with a maximal PL atlas where a PL atlas is an atlas in which the transition maps are PL.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=A [[PL space]] is a space with a locally finite simplicial triangulation.}}

{{term|Poincaré}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Henri Poincaré]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[Poincaré duality theorem]] says: given a manifold ''M'' of dimension ''n'' and an abelian group ''A'', there is a natural isomorphism
:<math>\operatorname{H}^*_c(M; A) \simeq \operatorname{H}_{n - *}(M; A)</math>.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Poincaré conjecture]]}}
{{defn|no=4|1=[[Poincaré lemma]] states the higher de Rham cohomology of a contractible smooth manifold vanishes.}}
{{defn|no=5|1=[[Poincaré homology sphere]].}}

{{term|Pontrjagin–Thom construction}}

{{term|Postnikov system}}
{{defn|1=A [[Postnikov system]] is a sequence of fibrations, such that all preceding manifolds have vanishing [[homotopy group]]s below a given dimension.}}

{{term|principal fibration}}
{{defn|1=Usually synonymous with [[G-fibration|''G''-fibration]].}}

{{term|prime decomposition}}

{{term|profinite}}
{{defn|1=[[profinite homotopy theory]]; it studies [[profinite space]]s.}}

{{term|properly discontinuous}}
{{defn|Not particularly a precise term. But it could mean, for example, that ''G'' is discrete and each point of the ''G''-space has a neighborhood ''V'' such that for each ''g'' in ''G'' that is not the identity element, ''gV'' intersects ''V'' at finitely many points.}}

{{term|pseudomanifold}}
{{defn|[[pseudomanifold]]}}

{{term|pullback}}
{{defn|1=Given a map ''p'':''E''→''B'', the [[pullback (topology)|pullback]] of ''p'' along ''ƒ'':''X''→''B'' is the space <math>f^*E = \{ (e, x) \in E \times X | p(e) = f(x) \}</math> (succinctly it is the [[equalizer (mathematics)|equalizer]] of ''p'' and ''f''). It is a space over ''X'' through a projection.}}

{{term|Puppe sequence}}
{{defn|1=The [[Puppe sequence]] refers ro either of the sequences
::<math>X \overset{f}\to Y \to C_f \to \Sigma X \to \Sigma Y \to \cdots,</math>
::<math>\cdots \to \Omega X \to \Omega Y \to F_f \to X \overset{f}\to Y</math>
:where <math>C_f, F_f</math> are homotopy cofiber and homotopy fiber of ''f''.}}

{{term|pushout}}
{{defn|1=Given <math>A \subset B</math> and a map <math>f: A \to X</math>, the [[pushout (topology)|pushout]] of ''X'' and ''B'' along ''f'' is
::<math>X \cup_f B = X \sqcup B/(a \sim f(a))</math>;
:that is ''X'' and ''B'' are glued together along ''A'' through ''f''. The map ''f'' is usually called the attaching map.

:An important example is when ''B'' = ''D''<sup>''n''</sup>, ''A'' = ''S''<sup>''n''-1</sup>; in that case, forming such a pushout is called attaching an ''n''-cell (meaning an ''n''-disk) to ''X''.}}

{{glossary end}}

== Q ==
{{glossary}}
{{term|quasi-fibration}}
{{defn|1=A [[quasi-fibration]] is a map such that the fibers are homotopy equivalent to each other.}}

{{term|Quillen}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Daniel Quillen]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=Quillen’s theorem says that <math>\pi_* MU</math> is the [[Lazard ring]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== R ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|rational}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[rational homotopy theory]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[rationalization (algebraic topology)|rationalization]] of a space ''X'' is, roughly, the [[localization of a space|localization]] of ''X'' at zero. More precisely, ''X''<sub>0</sub> together with ''j'': ''X'' → ''X''<sub>0</sub> is a rationalization of ''X'' if the map <math>\pi_* X \otimes \mathbb{Q} \to \pi_* X_0 \otimes \mathbb{Q}</math> induced by ''j'' is an isomorphism of vector spaces and <math>\pi_* X_0 \otimes \mathbb{Q} \simeq \pi_* X_0</math>.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The [[rational homotopy type]] of ''X'' is the weak homotopy type of ''X''<sub>0</sub>.}}
{{defn|no=4|1=A [[rational homology manifold]].}}

{{term|regulator}}
{{defn|no=1|[[Borel regulator]].}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Beilinson regulator]].}}

{{term|Reidemeister}}
{{defn|1=[[Reidemeister torsion]].}}

{{term|reduced}}
{{defn|1=The [[reduced suspension]] of a based space ''X'' is the smash product <math>\Sigma X = X \wedge S^1</math>. It is related to the [[loop functor]] by <math>\operatorname{Map}(\Sigma X, Y) = \operatorname{Map}(X, \Omega Y)</math> where <math>\Omega Y = \operatorname{Map}(S^1, Y)</math> is the loop space.}}

{{term|resolution}}
{{defn|A [[resolution (topology)|resolution]] of a space ''X'' is a map <math>M \to X</math> from a topological or smooth manifold that is locally a homotopy equivalence. A space is resolvable if it admits a reoslution.}}

{{term|retract}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[retraction (topology)|retract]] of a map ''f'' is a map ''r'' such that <math>r \circ f</math> is the identity (in other words, ''f'' is a section of ''r'').}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A subspace <math>A \subset X</math> is called a retract if the inclusion map <math>A \hookrightarrow X</math> admits a retract (see [[#deformation retract]]).}}

{{term|ring spectrum}}
{{defn|1=A [[ring spectrum]] is a spectrum satisfying the ring axioms, either on nose or up to homotopy. For example, a [[complex K-theory]] is a ring spectrum.}}

{{term|Rokhlin}}
{{defn|[[Rokhlin invariant]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== S ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Samelson product}}

{{term|Schoenflies}}
{{defn|[[Schoenflies problem]]}}

{{term|Serre}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Jean-Pierre Serre]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Serre class]].}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Serre spectral sequence]].}}

{{term|shape}}
{{defn|1=[[Shape theory (mathematics)|Shape theory]].}}

{{term|simple}}

{{term|simple-homotopy equivalence}}
{{defn|A map ƒ:''X''→''Y'' between finite simplicial complexes (e.g., manifolds) is a [[simple-homotopy equivalence]] if it is homotopic to a composition of finitely many [[elementary expansion]]s and [[elementary collapse]]s. A homotopy equivalence is a simple-homotopy equivalence if and only if its [[Whitehead torsion]] vanishes.}}

{{term|simplicial approximation}}
{{defn|1=See [[simplicial approximation theorem]].}}

{{term|simplicial complex}}
{{defn|1=See [[simplicial complex]]; the basic example is a triangulation of a manifold.}}

{{term|simplicial homology}}
{{defn|1=A [[simplicial homology]] is the (canonical) homology of a simplicial complex. Note it applies to simplicial complexes and not to spaces; cf. [[#singular homology]].}}

{{term|signature invariant}}

{{term|singular}}
{{defn|no=1|1=Given a space ''X'' and an abelian group π, the [[singular homology group]] of ''X'' with coefficients in π is
:<math>\operatorname{H}_*(X; \pi) = \operatorname{H}_*(C_*(X) \otimes \pi)</math>
where <math>C_*(X)</math> is the [[singular chain complex]] of ''X''; i.e., the ''n''-th degree piece is the free abelian group generated by all the maps <math>\triangle^n \to X</math> from the standard ''n''-simplex to ''X''. A singular homology is a special case of a [[simplicial homology]]; indeed, for each space ''X'', there is the [[singular simplicial complex]] of ''X'' <ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/singular+simplicial+complex|title = Singular simplicial complex in nLab}}</ref> whose homology is the singular homology of ''X''.}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[singular simplices functor]] is the functor <math>\mathbf{Top} \to s\mathbf{Set}</math> from the category of all spaces to the category of simplicial sets, that is the right adjoint to the [[geometric realization functor]].}}
{{defn|no=3|The '''singular simplicial complex''' of a space ''X'' is the [[normalized chain complex]] of the singular simplex of ''X''.}}

{{term|slant product}}

{{term|small object argument}}

{{term|smash product}}
{{defn|1=The [[smash product]] of based spaces ''X'', ''Y'' is <math>X \wedge Y = X \times Y / X \vee Y</math>. It is characterized by the adjoint relation
:<math>\operatorname{Map}(X \wedge Y, Z) = \operatorname{Map}(X, \operatorname{Map}(Y, Z))</math>.}}

{{term|Spanier–Whitehead}}
{{defn|1=The [[Spanier–Whitehead duality]].}}

{{term|spectrum}}
{{defn|1=Roughly a sequence of spaces together with the maps (called the structure maps) between the consecutive terms; see [[spectrum (topology)]].}}

{{term|sphere bundle}}
{{defn|1=A [[sphere bundle]] is a fiber bundle whose fibers are spheres.}}

{{term|sphere spectrum}}
{{defn|The [[sphere spectrum]] is a spectrum consisting of a sequence of spheres <math>S^0, S^1, S^2, S^3, \dots</math> together with the maps between the spheres given by suspensions. In short, it is the [[suspension spectrum]] of <math>S^0</math>.}}

{{term|Spivak}}
{{defn|[[Spivak normal fibration]]}}

{{term|stable homotopy group}}
{{defn|1=See [[#homotopy group]].}}

{{term|Steenrod homology}}
{{defn|1=[[Steenrod homology]].}}

{{term|Steenrod operation}}

{{term|Sullivan}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Dennis Sullivan]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[Sullivan conjecture]].}}
{{defn|no=3|1={{citation| title=Infinitesimal computations in topology|journal=Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS|year=1977|volume=47|pages=269–331|url=http://www.numdam.org/item?id=PMIHES_1977__47__269_0|last1=Sullivan|first1=Dennis|doi=10.1007/BF02684341|s2cid=42019745}} - introduces [[rational homotopy theory]] (along with Quillen's paper).}}
{{defn|no=4|The [[Sullivan algebra]] in the rational homotopy theory.}}

{{term|super}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[superspace]] is a locally ringed space whose structure sheaf is a sheaf of [[superring]]s.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[supermanifold]].}}

{{term|suspension spectrum}}
{{defn|The [[suspension spectrum]] of a based space ''X'' is the spectrum given by <math>X_n = \Sigma^n X</math>.}}

{{term|stratified}}
{{defn|no=1|A [[stratified space]] is a topological space with a stratification.}}
{{defn|no=2|A [[stratified Morse theory]] is a Morse theory done on a stratified space.}}

{{term|symmetric spectrum}}
{{defn|1=See [[symmetric spectrum]].}}

{{term|symplectic topology}}
{{defn|1=[[symplectic topology]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== T ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Tate}}
{{defn|[[Tate sphere]]}}

{{term|telescope}}

{{term|Thom}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[René Thom]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=If ''E'' is a vector bundle on a paracompact space ''X'', then the [[Thom space]] <math>\text{Th}(E)</math> of ''E'' is obtained by first replacing each fiber by its compactification and then collapsing the base ''X''.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=The [[Thom isomorphism]] says: for each [[orientable vector bundle]] ''E'' of rank ''n'' on a manifold ''X'', a choice of an orientation (the [[Thom class]] of ''E'') induces an isomorphism
:<math>\widetilde{\operatorname{H}}^{*+n}(\text{Th}(E); \mathbb{Z})\simeq \operatorname{H}^*(X; \mathbb{Z})</math>.}}
{{defn|no=4|1=[[Thom's first isotopy lemma|Thom's first]] and [[Thom's second isotopy lemma|second]] isotopy lemmas.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://mathoverflow.net/questions/304298/thoms-first-isotopy-lemma | title=Differential topology - Thom's first isotopy lemma }}</ref>}}
{{defn|no=5|1=A [[Thom mapping]] originally called a mapping "sans éclatement"}}

{{term|topological chiral homology}}

{{term|topological fundamental group}}

{{term|transfer}}

{{term|transgression}}

{{term|triangulation}}
{{defn|[[triangulation]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== U ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|universal coefficient}}
{{defn|1=The [[universal coefficient theorem]].}}

{{term|up to homotopy}}
{{defn|1=A statement holds in the [[homotopy category]] as opposed to the category of spaces.}}

{{glossary end}}

== V ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|V-manifold}}
{{defn|An old term for an [[orbifold]].}}

{{term|van Kampen}}
{{defn|1=The [[van Kampen theorem]] says: if a space ''X'' is path-connected and if ''x''<sub>0</sub> is a point in ''X'', then
:<math>\pi_1(X, x_0) = \varinjlim \pi_1(U, x_0)</math>
where the [[colimit]] runs over some open cover of ''X'' consisting of path-connected open subsets containing ''x''<sub>0</sub> such that the cover is closed under finite intersections.}}

{{term|Verdier}}
{{defn|[[Verdier duality]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== W ==

{{glossary}}
{{term|Waldhausen S-construction}}
{{defn|1=[[Waldhausen S-construction]].}}

{{term|Wall's finiteness obstruction}}

{{term|Warsaw}}
{{defn|1=The [[Warsaw circle]] gives an important counterexample to the Whitehead theorem.}}

{{term|weak equivalence}}
{{defn|1=A map ƒ:''X''→''Y'' of based spaces is a [[weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak equivalence]] if for each ''q'', the induced map <math>f_*: \pi_q X \to \pi_q Y</math> is bijective.}}

{{term|wedge}}
{{defn|1=For based spaces ''X'', ''Y'', the [[wedge product (topology)|wedge product]] <math>X \wedge Y</math> of ''X'' and ''Y'' is the [[coproduct (category theory)|coproduct]] of ''X'' and ''Y''; concretely, it is obtained by taking their disjoint union and then identifying the respective base points.}}

{{term|well pointed}}
{{defn|1=A based space is [[well pointed space|well pointed]] (or non-degenerately based) if the inclusion of the base point is a cofibration.}}

{{term|Whitehead}}
{{defn|no=1|[[J. H. C. Whitehead]].}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Whitehead's theorem]] says that for [[CW complexes]], the [[homotopy equivalence]] is the same thing as the [[weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak equivalence]].}}
{{defn|no=3|[[Whitehead torsion|Whitehead group]].}}
{{defn|no=4|[[Whitehead product]].}}

{{term|winding number}}
{{defn|no=1|[[winding number]].}}

{{term|Witt}}
{{defn|1=[[Witt space]].}}

{{glossary end}}
